0.comment: Xilonen: Tumaini, the Traveler's Ancient Name
0.content: In 5.0, after the Traveler helped rescue Kachina, Mavuika promised them an Ancient Name and handed the job to Xilonen, telling her only that it would be for "a traveler" and "quite difficult". In 5.1 Xilonen discovered the recipient was an outlander. The Night Kingdom records only Natlanese deeds, so a Name seemed impossible, but she took the task as proof of Mavuika's trust and a test of her own skill. She wrote to Citlali, and the two took the problem to the Lord of the Night, who created the Pilgrim's Chronicle to record the Traveler's deeds in Natlan. In the 5.2 Interlude Xilonen gathered people's stories of the Traveler before the Chronicle, with Paimon finishing it; in 5.3 she forged the Name within the three days before Mavuika's planned descent. It is Tumaini, "hope", the first ever borne by an outlander.

1.comment: Xilonen: The Price of Forging a Name
1.content: That night in 5.1, Xilonen and Citlali visited the Lord of the Night. Asked whether the Traveler deserved a Name, Xilonen said they were special, had saved Kachina, and that Natlan owed them a debt a Name could at least protect. The Lord asked if she would pay with her own life. She said yes. The Lord explained that a new Name is like a seed and the Engraver's life is the outer shell that shields it until it takes root in the Night Kingdom, then gradually disappears. Xilonen called the sacrifice "practically negligible" if it gave Natlan a future, and said she would not regret it: "I bear the name 'Baraka.' This is a part of my duty."

2.content: Mavuika considers Xilonen one of the best craftsmen in Natlan, "well-versed in Secret Source technology", and admires that she never backs away from a challenge. Xilonen's view of their dealings: "ridiculous commissions." Mavuika wanted a sword that would not melt in her flames, sunglasses to see enemies through fire, and above all a phlogiston-powered vehicle. She kept showing up with dragon design schematics of unknown origin until Xilonen gave in. The Flamestrider took three whole months. Compared with all that, Xilonen says, an Ancient Name for an outlander was "a relatively reasonable task".

3.content: Teyiz was a renowned, kindly Name Engraver who taught the Children of Echoes' children. Xilonen was her one student who stayed awake through technical classes, firing off questions about phlogiston (could you cook meat by dropping it down a phlogiston-filled chimney?). She skipped the hero-story classes with excuses. Teyiz saw through them and told her that for Name Engravers, stories and equations are one and the same. In story classes Teyiz asked how an Engraver would choose between conflicting versions of a legend, and set the children to trace evidence across records. That approach won Xilonen over.

4.content: Tlazolli, bearer of the Ancient Name Undugu, was a celebrated Name Engraver Xilonen grew up admiring and calls "Auntie". Her daughter Nechca died in an Abyss attack years ago. Tlazolli took in Nepecha, an orphan from the same attack born on the same day, and passed her off as Nechca recovering from illness and memory loss. Xilonen, who thought of herself as Nechca's pen-pal big sister, visited with a book Nechca had asked for. She found that Tlazolli's popular Blazegem Inscriptions were near-Ancient Names secretly draining the tribe's memories of Nechca. Tlazolli meant to overwrite Nepecha's mind with them.

5.comment: Xilonen: Ancient Names and the Name Engraver's craft
5.content: Ancient Names carry past heroes' legacies. Each comes as a feather-shaped obsidian stone, and the Wayob grant them to those who have "done something in their lifetime that exemplifies the 'spirit' of the Name." The Children of Echoes believe only their tribe can bear the duty of forging them. Xilonen says the technique is simple; the hard part is verifying deeds whose witnesses are long dead. She uses the Masters of the Night-Wind's woven scrolls, Citlali's knowledge and contacts across the six tribes, cross-referencing every link. A falsehood makes a Name "seriously defective" and can cause cognitive problems for its bearer. Names can also be forged from a deserving person's life after death, and the Wayob choose who receives them.
